cards.title: Polynomial-time EFX for three additive agents
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k≥1 such that, for every finite set of goods and every three nonnegative rational additive valuations, A returns a complete EFX allocation in at most C(N+1)^k steps, where N is the binary input length and EFX has the all-goods convention below?
cards.why: The smallest unresolved computational case for exact EFX after existence for three agents was established.

progress.text: Complete EFX existence for three additive agents is proved constructively, with a pseudopolynomial algorithm.
Polynomial-time EF2X for three agents is obtained, while the paper explicitly retains the exact EFX computational gap.
A preprint reports polynomial-time approximate EFX for up to eight agents, a different guarantee from exact EFX.

cards.definitions: There are exactly three agents, indexed 1,2,3, and m≥0 goods indexed by [m]={1,…,m}. The input gives m and each value v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 encoded in binary. N is the total bit length of this explicit table and its delimiters. For any bundle S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. A complete allocation is an ordered partition (A₁,A₂,A₃) of [m]; bundles may be empty. The output assigns each good one owner in {1,2,3}. It is EFX if v_i(A_i)≥v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every i,j∈{1,2,3} and every g∈A_j, including goods with v_i,g=0. The removed good is evaluated by agent i. An empty A_j gives no inequality; a singleton leaves the empty bundle of value zero. Removal is hypothetical and does not discard a good from the output. Values may have arbitrary magnitudes and denominators. The algorithm is uniform, deterministic and always correct, with ordinary bit-operation cost and no oracle, payments or divisible goods. Its running time must be polynomial in N, not in the numeric values.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives an algorithm and proves completeness, every EFX inequality, and a worst-case polynomial bit bound on all inputs. A negative answer proves that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists. Existence alone is already established for this three-agent additive model; a particular unfair allocation, pseudopolynomial runtime or a relaxed fairness guarantee does not answer the computational question.

context_blocks.title: Every possible removed good matters
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods in another bundle at 5 and 1. Removing the good worth 5 would remove her envy, but removing the one worth 1 would leave value 5, still above 4. This pair passes the weaker “some good” test of EF1 and fails EFX. The test always uses the envious agent’s values, since the agents may disagree about an item’s worth.

context_blocks.title: Existence has already been proved
context_blocks.text: Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn establish complete EFX allocations for three additive agents. Their definition tests all goods, and their perturbation lemma handles zero values and ties. Thus this card asks how efficiently such an allocation can be found. The general existence card TCS-0011 concerns more agents and uses its explicitly stated positive-good convention.

context_blocks.title: Why pseudopolynomial time is insufficient
context_blocks.text: A value as large as 2^L needs only L+1 binary digits. An algorithm whose time grows polynomially in that value may therefore take exponentially many steps in its encoding length. The inherited question requires a bound polynomial in the complete valuation table’s bit length, including denominators. It does not require the stronger guarantee that the number of arithmetic operations be independent of value bit lengths.

context_blocks.title: Nearby guarantees do not give exact EFX
context_blocks.text: Ashuri, Gkatzelis and Sgouritsa’s 2025 result computes EF2X for three agents in polynomial time: envy disappears after removing any two goods, a weaker requirement. Their paper explicitly leaves exact EFX at the pseudopolynomial frontier. The May 2026 preprint reports improved multiplicative approximations, including 2/3-EFX for up to eight agents; this also permits remaining envy and does not settle exact EFX for three.

sentences: Three agents must receive all indivisible goods under nonnegative additive valuations.
An allocation is EFX when removing any one good from another agent’s bundle would eliminate the first agent’s envy.
Such allocations are known to exist for three agents, including when values are zero or tied.
The question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the binary valuation table’s length.
Pseudopolynomial constructions and polynomial algorithms for weaker fairness guarantees do not settle this target.

cards.context:
Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods in another bundle at 5 and 1. Removing the good worth 5 would remove her envy, but removing the one worth 1 would leave value 5, still above 4. This pair passes the weaker “some good” test of EF1 and fails EFX. The test always uses the envious agent’s values, since the agents may disagree about an item’s worth.

Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn establish complete EFX allocations for three additive agents. Their definition tests all goods, and their perturbation lemma handles zero values and ties. Thus this card asks how efficiently such an allocation can be found. The general existence card TCS-0011 concerns more agents and uses its explicitly stated positive-good convention.

A value as large as 2^L needs only L+1 binary digits. An algorithm whose time grows polynomially in that value may therefore take exponentially many steps in its encoding length. The inherited question requires a bound polynomial in the complete valuation table’s bit length, including denominators. It does not require the stronger guarantee that the number of arithmetic operations be independent of value bit lengths.

Ashuri, Gkatzelis and Sgouritsa’s 2025 result computes EF2X for three agents in polynomial time: envy disappears after removing any two goods, a weaker requirement. Their paper explicitly leaves exact EFX at the pseudopolynomial frontier. The May 2026 preprint reports improved multiplicative approximations, including 2/3-EFX for up to eight agents; this also permits remaining envy and does not settle exact EFX for three.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
